claim: Computation in neural circuits relies on the judicious use of nonlinear circuit components.
source: Computation in neural circuits relies on the judicious use of nonlinear circuit components.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural computation presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript.

claim: Multiple nonlinear components work collectively to control circuit outputs in many cases.
source: In many cases, multiple nonlinear components work collectively to control circuit outputs.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural circuits presented in the abstract.

claim: Separating the contributions of different nonlinear components is difficult.
source: Separating the contributions of these different components is difficult, and this limits our understanding of the mechanistic basis of many important computations.
evidence: This statement describes a limitation in the field based on established understanding.

claim: A tool has been introduced that permits the design of light stimuli that predictably alter rod and cone phototransduction currents.
source: Here, we introduce a tool that permits the design of light stimuli that predictably alter rod and cone phototransduction currents – including stimuli that compensate for nonlinear properties such as light adaptation.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by experimental demonstrations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The tool can design stimuli that compensate for nonlinear properties such as light adaptation.
source: Here, we introduce a tool that permits the design of light stimuli that predictably alter rod and cone phototransduction currents – including stimuli that compensate for nonlinear properties such as light adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6-10.

claim: The tool is based on well-established models for the rod and cone phototransduction cascade.
source: This tool, based on well-established models for the rod and cone phototransduction cascade, permits the separation of nonlinearities in phototransduction from those in downstream circuits.
evidence: The manuscript builds on existing phototransduction models cited throughout.

claim: The tool permits the separation of nonlinearities in phototransduction from those in downstream circuits.
source: This tool, based on well-established models for the rod and cone phototransduction cascade, permits the separation of nonlinearities in phototransduction from those in downstream circuits.
evidence: This capability is demonstrated in Figure 10 with horizontal cells and bipolar cells.

claim: The tool will allow direct tests of how adaptation in rod and cone phototransduction affects downstream visual signals and perception.
source: This will allow, for example, direct tests of how adaptation in rod and cone phototransduction affects downstream visual signals and perception.
evidence: This is a prospective claim about future applications, supported by the demonstrated capability in the manuscript.

claim: Behaviorally significant computations typically rely on a diverse collection of interacting circuit mechanisms, many of which are nonlinear.
source: Such computations typically rely on a diverse collection of interacting circuit mechanisms, many of which are nonlinear (Gollisch and Meister, 2010; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Jadzinsky and Baccus, 2013; Zador, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Circuit outputs typically do not uniquely identify the role of specific circuit mechanisms.
source: Circuit outputs – which are often most amenable to experimental measurement – typically do not uniquely identify the role of specific circuit mechanisms.
evidence: This is a general statement about the challenge in neuroscience based on established understanding.

claim: Models for retinal processing generally assume that photoreceptor responses are linear or near linear, despite decades of direct evidence that this is not the case.
source: For example, models for retinal processing generally assume that photoreceptor responses are linear or near linear, despite decades of direct evidence that this is not the case (reviewed by Burns and Baylor, 2001; Schwartz, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Both photoreceptors and post-photoreceptor circuits adjust response properties such as gain and kinetics to match the prevailing light inputs.
source: Both photoreceptors and post-photoreceptor circuits adjust response properties such as gain and kinetics to match the prevailing light inputs (reviewed by Demb, 2008; Dunn and Rieke, 2006)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Models for retinal outputs typically start by passing light inputs through a linear spatio-temporal filter.
source: yet models for retinal outputs typically start by passing light inputs through a linear spatio-temporal filter; this architecture includes linear–nonlinear (Chichilnisky, 2001), generalized-linear (Pillow et al., 2008), and computational neural network (CNN) (McIntosh et al., 2016; Turner et al., 2019) models.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific modeling approaches.

claim: Models with an initial linear filtering stage cannot capture the spatially local adaptation produced by photoreceptors.
source: Models with an initial linear filtering stage cannot capture the spatially local adaptation produced by photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the properties of linear models and photoreceptor adaptation.

claim: Existing phototransduction models, with appropriate parameters, can account for responses of rod and cone photoreceptors from both primate and mouse to a broad range of inputs.
source: We show that existing phototransduction models, with appropriate parameters, can account for responses of rod and cone photoreceptors from both primate and mouse to a broad range of inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The phototransduction models can be mathematically inverted to enable the design of stimuli that will elicit photoreceptor responses with specific desired properties.
source: We then show that these models can be mathematically inverted – enabling the design of stimuli that will elicit photoreceptor responses with specific desired properties such as a linear dependence on light input.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical derivation and experimental validation in Figures 3-9.

claim: Direct recordings of responses to inverted stimuli show that they work as designed.
source: Direct recordings of responses to these stimuli show that they work as designed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6-9.

claim: A biochemical model architecture was chosen because it was more clearly connected to the mechanistic operation of the phototransduction cascade than empirical models.
source: We chose this model rather than empirical models (e.g. Clark et al., 2013) because it was more clearly connected to the mechanistic operation of the phototransduction cascade and because it was exactly invertible (see Angueyra et al., 2022 for comparison of the biochemical model with empirical models).
evidence: This is a methodological choice explained by the authors, with citation to comparison work.

claim: The biochemical model was chosen because it was exactly invertible.
source: We chose this model rather than empirical models (e.g. Clark et al., 2013) because it was more clearly connected to the mechanistic operation of the phototransduction cascade and because it was exactly invertible (see Angueyra et al., 2022 for comparison of the biochemical model with empirical models).
evidence: This is a methodological choice with mathematical justification provided in the Methods.

claim: The phototransduction current flows through cGMP-gated channels in the photoreceptor outer segment.
source: In brief, the phototransduction current flows through cGMP-gated channels in the photoreceptor outer segment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phototransduction, supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Levels of cGMP, and hence the phototransduction current, are maximal in darkness.
source: Levels of cGMP, and hence the phototransduction current, are maximal in darkness.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phototransduction.

claim: Light activates G-protein-coupled receptors, which activate G-proteins and a cGMP-phosphodiesterase (PDE).
source: Light activates G-protein-coupled receptors, which activate G-proteins and a cGMP-phosphodiesterase (PDE).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the phototransduction cascade.

claim: The decrease in cGMP concentration allows some cGMP-gated channels to close and decreases the current.
source: The resulting decrease in cGMP concentration allows some cGMP-gated channels to close and decreases the current.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phototransduction.

claim: Levels of cGMP are restored by synthesis of cGMP by a guanylate cyclase.
source: Levels of cGMP are restored by synthesis of cGMP by a guanylate cyclase
evidence: This is established knowledge about phototransduction.

claim: Cyclase activity is sped by a calcium-feedback pathway that strongly shapes light responses.
source: cyclase activity is sped by a calcium-feedback pathway that strongly shapes light responses (Burns et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The phototransduction model has a total of 11 parameters.
source: Our phototransduction model has a total of 11 parameters (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Two model parameters (q and Smax) can be expressed in terms of others using steady state conditions.
source: Two of these (q and Smax) can be expressed in terms of others using steady state conditions – for example the constraint that dC(t)/dt = 0 in steady state.
evidence: This is a mathematical constraint explained in the text.

claim: Several model parameters were fixed based on previous measurements and their relatively minor impact on model predictions, including k, n, and m for both rods and cones and β for rods.
source: Several others were fixed based on previous measurements and their relatively minor impact on model predictions; this included k, n, and m for both rods and cones (Koutalos et al., 1995b; Rieke and Baylor, 1996) and β for rods (Field and Rieke, 2002).
evidence: This is a methodological choice supported by citations to prior measurements.

claim: The dark cGMP concentration was estimated from the measured dark current for each recorded cell.
source: The dark cGMP concentration was estimated from the measured dark current for each recorded cell.
evidence: This describes a data-driven parameter estimation procedure.

claim: The receptor and PDE decay rates (σ and Φ) had near identical effects on predictions and were constrained to be equal.
source: The receptor and PDE decay rates (σ and Φ) had near identical effects on predictions (see Pugh and Lamb, 1993) and were constrained to be equal.
evidence: This is a modeling constraint based on prior work and model behavior.

claim: The number of free model parameters was reduced to 4 for rods and 5 for cones.
source: These considerations allowed us to reduce the number of free model parameters to 4 for rods and 5 for cones.
evidence: This is stated directly as a result of the parameter constraints.

claim: The free parameters for rod models consisted of the gain γ, the photopigment decay rate σ, the spontaneous PDE activation rate η, and the constant KGC specifying the calcium sensitivity of the cGMP synthesis rate.
source: The free parameters consisted of the gain γ with which photons are converted to photopigment activity, the photopigment decay rate σ, the spontaneous PDE activation rate η, the constant KGC specifying the calcium sensitivity of the cGMP synthesis rate, and (for cones) the rate β of Ca2+ extrusion.
evidence: This explicitly lists the free parameters for the model.

claim: For cone models, the free parameters included an additional parameter β, the rate of Ca2+ extrusion.
source: The free parameters consisted of the gain γ with which photons are converted to photopigment activity, the photopigment decay rate σ, the spontaneous PDE activation rate η, the constant KGC specifying the calcium sensitivity of the cGMP synthesis rate, and (for cones) the rate β of Ca2+ extrusion.
evidence: This explicitly lists the free parameters for cone models.

claim: Optimal values for free parameters were numerically identified separately for each photoreceptor type.
source: We numerically identified optimal values for these parameters separately for each photoreceptor type (see Methods).
evidence: This describes the fitting procedure used.

claim: Rod photoreceptors were recorded using suction electrodes, which allow for stable, long-lasting recordings.
source: We recorded from rod photoreceptors using suction electrodes, which allow for stable, long-lasting recordings.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: Responses to a comprehensive set of stimuli were measured from each individual rod.
source: This allowed us to measure responses to a comprehensive set of stimuli from each individual rod.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach enabled by the recording method.

claim: Cone photoreceptors were recorded using whole-cell patch clamp recordings.
source: We recorded from cone photoreceptors using whole-cell patch clamp recordings.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for cones.

claim: Light responses in cone recordings are stable for a much shorter time than rod recordings due to internal dialysis.
source: Light responses are stable in these recordings for a much shorter time (due to internal dialysis)
evidence: This explains a limitation of the cone recording method.

claim: Responses to a single stimulus type were recorded from each individual cone.
source: and consequently we recorded responses to a single stimulus type from each individual cone.
evidence: This describes the experimental constraint for cone recordings.

claim: A common model with the same parameters fit responses of a mouse rod photoreceptor across stimuli.
source: Nonetheless, a common model specified by four free parameters (γ, σ, η, and KGC) accounts for many aspects of the responses to this set of stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fits shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Best-fit parameters varied by approximately 10% across different photoreceptors.
source: These parameters were well constrained by fitting the measured responses: best-fit parameters varied by ~10% across different photoreceptors
evidence: This describes the variability in fitted parameters across cells.

claim: The MSE increased significantly for 10-20% changes in parameters.
source: and the MSE increased significantly for 10–20% changes in parameters (see Methods for a more detailed analysis).
evidence: This indicates that parameters are well-constrained by the data.

claim: Consensus parameters for mouse and primate rods were very similar.
source: Consensus parameters for mouse and primate rods were very similar (see Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the parameter values shown in Table 1.

claim: Consensus parameters for mouse and primate cones differed substantially, reflecting the approximately twofold faster kinetics of primate cone responses.
source: Consensus parameters for mouse and primate cones differed substantially, reflecting the ~twofold faster kinetics of primate cone responses (flash response time-to-peak is ~35 ms in primate cones, and ~70 ms in mouse cones; see Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the parameter values in Table 1 and kinetic measurements.

claim: The consensus models captured the measured responses well.
source: The resulting models (red) captured the measured responses (black) well.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: Consensus models captured more than 80% of the variance of the responses for each recorded cell.
source: For each recorded cell, the consensus models captured more than 80% of the variance of the responses (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is shown quantitatively in Figure 2B.

claim: On average, consensus models captured approximately 90% of the variance.
source: on average these models captured ~90% of the variance.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Consensus models and models fit to individual cells performed similarly.
source: Consensus models and models fit to individual cells performed similarly (Figure 2B).
evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Models generalized well across stimuli and to cells that did not contribute to the fits.
source: Models also generalized well across stimuli and to cells that did not contribute to the fits (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rod and cone phototransduction currents depend linearly on light intensity for low-contrast inputs.
source: Rod and cone phototransduction currents depend linearly on light intensity for low-contrast inputs (e.g. Baylor et al., 1984; Hass et al., 2015; Schnapf et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Linear predictions deviated from the measured responses considerably more than did predictions of the biochemical model.
source: Linear predictions deviated from the measured responses considerably more than did predictions of our biochemical model (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown quantitatively in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Linear models overpredicted responses at high mean light levels.
source: Specifically, linear models overpredicted responses at high mean light levels, and underpredicted responses at low mean light levels.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Linear models underpredicted responses at low mean light levels.
source: Specifically, linear models overpredicted responses at high mean light levels, and underpredicted responses at low mean light levels.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The biochemical model tracked the measured responses quite well.
source: The biochemical model, though not perfect, tracked the measured responses quite well.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The phototransduction model illustrated in Figure 1A can be exactly inverted to identify the stimulus that corresponds to a specific desired photoreceptor response.
source: In this section, we show that the model illustrated in Figure 1A can be exactly inverted to identify the stimulus that corresponds to a specific desired photoreceptor response.
evidence: This is demonstrated mathematically and experimentally in Figure 3.

claim: The result of model inversion is an estimate of the full stimulus in real units (isomerizations per second) corresponding to the desired response.
source: In other words, the result of model inversion is an estimate of the full stimulus in real units (isomerizations per second) corresponding to the desired response.
evidence: This describes the output of the inversion procedure.

claim: Model inversion requires a one-to-one relationship between inputs and outputs.
source: Model inversion requires a one-to-one relationship between inputs and outputs – that is for every input there must be a unique output and vice versa.
evidence: This is a mathematical requirement for invertibility.

claim: The phototransduction model consists of linear elements, static nonlinear elements, and a time-dependent nonlinear element.
source: Mathematically, this holds for the phototransduction model summarized in Figure 1A: the model consists of linear elements (Equations 1, 2, and 5), static nonlinear elements (Equations 4 and 6), and a time-dependent nonlinear element (Equation 3).
evidence: This describes the mathematical structure of the model.

claim: The linear elements can be described as linear filters and inverted by deconvolution.
source: The linear elements can be described as linear filters and inverted by deconvolution.
evidence: This is a standard mathematical property of linear systems.

claim: The static nonlinear elements consist of one-to-one mappings of inputs to outputs and can be inverted correspondingly.
source: The static nonlinear elements consist of one-to-one mappings of inputs to outputs and can be inverted correspondingly.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of monotonic functions.

claim: The time-dependent nonlinear component can be rearranged and solved analytically.
source: The time-dependent nonlinear component can be rearranged and solved analytically (see Methods).
evidence: The analytical solution is provided in the Methods section.

claim: The result is an analytical relationship between the phototransduction current and the stimulus.
source: The result is an analytical relationship between the phototransduction current and the stimulus – in other words an inverse model that takes the photocurrent as input and identifies the corresponding stimulus.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the mathematical inversion.

claim: The inversion procedure exactly recovers the stimulus that was used to generate a test current.
source: In this case, as expected, we recover exactly the stimulus that we started with, confirming that mathematically the phototransduction model can be inverted.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: Noise in the measured responses could cause the estimate to be better at some temporal frequencies than others.
source: Noise in the measured responses could cause the estimate to be better at some temporal frequencies than others; this is particularly true at high temporal frequencies that are poorly encoded by the photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a general principle of signal processing and deconvolution.

claim: High temporal frequencies are poorly encoded by the photoreceptors.
source: Noise in the measured responses could cause the estimate to be better at some temporal frequencies than others; this is particularly true at high temporal frequencies that are poorly encoded by the photoreceptors.
evidence: This is based on the known frequency response properties of photoreceptors.

claim: The frequency content of the stimulus was limited to temporal frequencies that could reasonably be expected to be recovered (0-60 Hz for primate cones, 0-30 Hz for mouse cones, 0-15 Hz for both primate and mouse rods).
source: we limited the frequency content of the stimulus to temporal frequencies that we could reasonably expect to recover (0–60 Hz for primate cones, 0–30 Hz for mouse cones, 0–15 Hz for both primate and mouse rods)
evidence: This describes a methodological constraint applied to improve estimates.

claim: The power spectrum of the estimated stimulus was required to match that of the true stimulus.
source: and required that the power spectrum of our estimate matched that of the true stimulus (see Methods).
evidence: This describes a constraint used to reduce noise in estimates.

claim: Stimulus estimates based on measured responses closely approximate the actual stimulus, including recovering rapid stimulus fluctuations.
source: The estimates closely approximate the actual stimulus, including recovering rapid stimulus fluctuations (insets).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A.

claim: For each photoreceptor type, stimulus estimates based on model inversion captured the majority of the stimulus variance.
source: For each photoreceptor type, stimulus estimates based on model inversion captured the majority of the stimulus variance (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown quantitatively in Figure 4B.

claim: At low temporal frequencies, stimulus power was much greater than that of the residuals, consistent with accurate stimulus estimation at these frequencies.
source: At low temporal frequencies, stimulus power was much greater than that of the residuals, consistent with accurate stimulus estimation at these frequencies.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: The stimulus and residual power spectra converged near 30 Hz for primate cones, 10 Hz for mouse cones, and 2-3 Hz for both primate and mouse rods.
source: This difference decreased with increasing frequency, and the two power spectra converged near 30 Hz for primate cones, 10 Hz for mouse cones, and 2–3 Hz for both primate and mouse rods.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: Adaptive nonlinearities in phototransduction cause the responses to sinusoidal light inputs to deviate from sinusoids.
source: Adaptive nonlinearities in phototransduction cause the responses to sinusoidal light inputs to deviate from sinusoids.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Time-dependent nonlinearities operate sufficiently rapidly to shape each cycle of the response.
source: These time-dependent nonlinearities operate sufficiently rapidly to shape each cycle of the response, causing responses to decreases in light intensity to be larger than those to increases and causing the responses to light-to-dark transitions to be slower than those to dark-to-light transitions.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Responses to decreases in light intensity are larger than those to increases.
source: causing responses to decreases in light intensity to be larger than those to increases
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Responses to light-to-dark transitions are slower than those to dark-to-light transitions.
source: and causing the responses to light-to-dark transitions to be slower than those to dark-to-light transitions.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Responses of both rod and cone photoreceptors to high-contrast sinusoidal light inputs are strongly nonsinusoidal.
source: As predicted by the model, responses of both rod and cone photoreceptors to high-contrast sinusoidal light inputs are strongly nonsinusoidal: responses to decreases in light intensity are larger than those to increases, and responses to dark-to-light transitions are faster than those to corresponding light-to-dark transitions (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Responses to the modified stimuli were much closer to sinusoidal than responses to the original sinusoidal stimuli.
source: Responses to the modified stimuli (red traces in Figure 7A) were much closer to sinusoidal than responses to the original sinusoidal stimuli (black traces).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7A.

claim: Asymmetries between increment and decrement responses and light-to-dark vs dark-to-light transitions were substantially reduced for the modified stimuli.
source: Specifically, asymmetries between increment and decrement responses and light-to-dark vs dark-to-light transitions were substantially reduced for the modified stimuli.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Sinusoidal fits to responses to the modified stimuli had considerably lower MSE than those to the original stimuli in each rod and cone tested.
source: Sinusoidal fits to responses to the modified stimuli had considerably lower MSE than those to the original stimuli in each rod and cone tested (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown quantitatively in Figure 7B.

claim: Neither the sinusoidal stimuli nor the specific cells that contribute to Figure 7 were used in fitting the phototransduction models.
source: Neither the sinusoidal stimuli nor the specific cells that contribute to Figure 7 were used in fitting the phototransduction models.
evidence: This describes the independence of the test data from the training data.

claim: Gain changes cause responses to a fixed strength flash to become smaller and faster when the mean light intensity increases.
source: These gain changes cause responses to a fixed strength flash to become smaller and faster when the mean light intensity increases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor adaptation.

claim: The response to the flash decreased approximately twofold at the higher mean light level for the control stimulus.
source: As expected, responses to this stimulus (black traces in Figure 8A) showed clear effects of adaptation. Specifically, the response to the flash decreased ~twofold at the higher mean light level (summarized in Figure 8B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A and quantified in Figure 8B.

claim: Responses to the test flashes had similar amplitudes at the low and high mean light level for the modified stimuli.
source: Responses to the test flashes had similar amplitudes at the low and high mean light level.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The change in gain produced by the background was reduced in all photoreceptor types for the modified stimuli.
source: The change in gain produced by the background was reduced in all photoreceptor types.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: None of the cells used to test the modified stimuli in Figure 8 contributed to the model fitting.
source: None of the cells used to test these modified stimuli contributed to the model fitting, so this again tests the ability of the models to generalize across photoreceptors.
evidence: This describes the independence of test data from training data.

claim: Changes in time-to-peak of the measured responses to the modified stimuli follow the predictions well for both rod and cone photoreceptors.
source: Changes in time-to-peak of the measured responses to the modified stimuli follow the predictions well for both rod and cone photoreceptors (summarized in Figure 9C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Speeding up responses by 20-30% is possible using the model inversion approach.
source: Nonetheless, speeding up responses by 20–30% is possible
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 9B.

claim: The time-to-peak of the measured responses closely follows predictions for both slowing and speeding manipulations.
source: As for slowing responses, the time-to-peak of the measured responses closely follows predictions (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The modified stimulus that negates cone adaptation effectively eliminated most or all of the adaptation in downstream responses of horizontal cells and On parasol ganglion cells.
source: Negating adaptation in the cones also eliminated most or all of the adaptation in downstream responses (summarized in Figure 10B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10A and quantified in Figure 10B.

claim: Horizontal cell responses to both original and modified stimuli showed clear nonlinearities.
source: Horizontal cell responses to both stimuli showed clear nonlinearities (Figure 10C, left); specifically, responses to the increment and decrement phases of the stimuli were highly asymmetric.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The depolarizing and hyperpolarizing phases of horizontal cell responses appeared more symmetrical for the modified stimuli.
source: The depolarizing and hyperpolarizing phases of the responses, however, appeared more symmetrical for the modified stimuli (red).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Compensating for nonlinearities in cone phototransduction reveals an additional, largely time-independent, nonlinear process shaping horizontal and cone bipolar responses.
source: In this case, compensating for nonlinearities in cone phototransduction reveals an additional, largely time-independent, nonlinear process shaping horizontal and cone bipolar responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 10C and D.

claim: The approach disentangles contributions of phototransduction and post-transduction processes to time-dependent and time-independent nonlinearities in the horizontal and bipolar responses.
source: Furthermore, it disentangles contributions of phototransduction and post-transduction processes to time-dependent and time-independent nonlinearities in the horizontal and bipolar responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 10C and D.

claim: The procedure used to invert the phototransduction cascade is only as good as the model upon which it is based.
source: The procedure that we use to invert the phototransduction cascade is only as good as the model upon which it is based.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the limitations of the approach.

claim: Consensus models were fit to recordings from one set of photoreceptors and then tested on different photoreceptors from different retinas.
source: We did this by fitting consensus models to recordings from one set of photoreceptors of a given type, and then testing the stimuli generated by these models on different photoreceptors from different retinas.
evidence: This describes the validation approach used.

claim: Systematic differences between predicted and measured responses were relatively small.
source: Systematic differences between predicted and measured responses were relatively small
evidence: This is observed across the validation experiments in Figures 6-9.

claim: Most of the differences between predicted and measured responses appear to reflect variability between cells.
source: and most of the differences appear to reflect variability between cells (e.g. due to cell-to-cell differences in sensitivity).
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of errors observed.

claim: The model describes the relationship between light inputs and phototransduction currents.
source: Our model describes the relationship between light inputs and phototransduction currents.
evidence: This defines the scope of the model.

claim: Consideration was restricted to photocurrents rather than photoreceptor synaptic output because the latter is shaped by several mechanisms that are less well understood than phototransduction.
source: We restricted our consideration to photocurrents rather than photoreceptor synaptic output because the latter is shaped by several mechanisms (e.g. electrical coupling between photoreceptors Copenhagen and Owen, 1976; Detwiler and Hodgkin, 1979; Schwartz, 1976 and horizontal feedback Baylor et al., 1971) that are less well understood than phototransduction.
evidence: This explains a limitation of the current approach with citations to relevant mechanisms.

claim: The model does not consider photopigment bleaching and regeneration via the pigment epithelium.
source: The model that we used does not consider photopigment bleaching and regeneration via the pigment epithelium.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the model.

claim: These aspects of photoreceptor function were omitted because the experiments require removal of the pigment epithelium.
source: We omitted these aspects of photoreceptor function because the experiments to which we fit and test the model require that we remove the pigment epithelium.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the limitation.

claim: Total light exposure in the experiments was restricted to minimize bleaching.
source: We restricted total light exposure in these experiments to minimize bleaching
evidence: This describes an experimental constraint.

claim: For rods, the model covers most or all of the range of rod signals because rod saturation occurs for light levels at which a small fraction of the rod pigment is bleached.
source: This is less of a concern for rods, where rod saturation occurs for light levels at which a small fraction of the rod pigment is bleached, and correspondingly our models cover most or all of the range of rod signals.
evidence: This explains why bleaching is less of a concern for rods.

claim: For cones, the model is limited to light levels less than 50,000 R*/s.
source: For cones, the model is limited to light levels <50,000 R*/s (similar to or a bit brighter than typical indoor lighting conditions).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the cone model.

claim: Speeding responses is particularly difficult because it requires increasing the amplitude of high temporal frequencies.
source: Speeding responses is particularly difficult because it requires increasing the amplitude of high temporal frequencies
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the signal processing required.

claim: The ability to speed responses is limited by the requirement that light intensities not assume negative values.
source: and the ability to do that is limited by the requirement that light intensities not assume negative values.
evidence: This is a physical constraint on the stimuli.

claim: Low-contrast stimuli can be sped more than high-contrast stimuli.
source: This means that low-contrast stimuli can be sped more than high-contrast stimuli.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the constraint on light intensities.

claim: The accuracy of the model predictions depends critically on accurate light calibrations.
source: The accuracy of the model predictions depends critically on accurate light calibrations.
evidence: This is a general principle of quantitative experiments.

claim: With consistent calibrations, the approaches used here should translate directly across laboratories and to in vivo physiological or perceptual studies.
source: With consistent calibrations, the approaches we use here should translate directly across laboratories and to in vivo physiological or perceptual studies.
evidence: This is a prediction about the generalizability of the approach.

claim: Time-dependent nonlinearities are particularly hard to capture in empirical models.
source: Time-dependent nonlinearities are particularly hard to capture in such models
evidence: This is based on the limitations of existing modeling approaches.

claim: Few existing models account for time-dependent nonlinearities.
source: and few existing models account for them.
evidence: This describes a limitation of current models.

claim: CNN models work best when stimulus parameters such as mean light intensity do not change.
source: As a result, these models work best when stimulus parameters such as mean light intensity do not change.
evidence: This is a known limitation of CNN models for visual responses.

claim: The photoreceptor models convert light inputs to photoreceptor responses, capturing time-dependent nonlinearities in this process.
source: The photoreceptor models described here convert light inputs to photoreceptor responses, capturing time-dependent nonlinearities in this process.
evidence: This describes the capability of the models developed in this work.

claim: A phototransduction model front end followed by an empirical model should decrease the demand placed on the empirical model and improve the ability to capture responses to stimuli that strongly engage photoreceptor adaptation.
source: This architecture – a phototransduction model front end followed by an empirical model – should decrease the demand placed on the empirical model and improve the ability to capture responses to stimuli that strongly engage photoreceptor adaptation.
evidence: This is a prediction about the benefits of the approach.
